title: How long to summarize a deposition on Mac: real hours, costs and fixes for lawyers
metaTitle: How long to summarize a deposition on a Mac, with real math
description: How long to summarize a deposition? Vendor estimates say 8 to 12 hours for a 3-hour deposition. Here are the math, costs and fixes for Mac lawyers.
targetKeyword: how long to summarize a deposition
secondaryKeywords: how long does a deposition summary take
intro: Plan on 8 to 12 hours of paralegal time for a 3-hour deposition, according to vendor estimates. A 200-page transcript at 20 to 25 pages an hour takes 8 to 10 hours to read and summarize. The clock often starts earlier than that work, because transcripts can take 7 to 14 business days to arrive. This page covers the math, the causes, and fixes you can use today without buying anything.
tldr: Vendor estimates put a paralegal summary of a 3-hour deposition at 8 to 12 hours.
A 200-page transcript at 20 to 25 pages an hour takes 8 to 10 hours of reading and summarizing.
The calendar is often the bigger delay, since transcripts can take 7 to 14 business days to arrive.
In one study, leading legal research AI tools hallucinated 17 to 33% of the time, so check every AI line against the transcript.
Follow your firm's rules on client data before you paste a transcript into any app.

blocks.text: How long does a deposition summary take?

The figure most people quote is 8 to 12 hours for a 3-hour deposition, done by a paralegal. It comes from a legal AI vendor's blog, and that vendor sells deposition analysis. The post cites no source for its numbers. We found no independent study that times deposition summaries. Use the range to plan, and treat it as a starting guess until you time your own work.
Turn transcript pages into hours

Start with the page count. Open the transcript, go to the last page, and write down the number. Then divide by a reading speed. The same paralegal blog gives 20 to 25 pages an hour as an industry average. That average has no named source, so measure your own speed on one section before you trust it.

blocks.caption: Simple arithmetic from the blog's reading speed and hourly rates. Not a measured result.

blocks.text: Those hours cover reading and summarizing only. They leave out the slow parts. A transcript full of exhibits takes longer than a clean one. Objections, errata sheets and cross-talk add minutes on many pages. Add a buffer to your estimate, and say so in your plan.
Why the calendar takes longer than the work

A 10-hour job rarely fits into a busy day, so it waits in a queue. Most of the delay happens before anyone reads a line. The same blog puts standard transcript turnaround at 7 to 14 business days. A deposition taken on a Monday can sit for a week or longer before a reader opens the file.
Ask your court reporter about turnaround when you book. Ask what delivery options exist and what they cost. Options vary by reporter and by case, so confirm them before you set the summary date.
Mistakes that make summaries take longer

items: Starting without a template. Every reader invents columns, so the draft gets rebuilt once it arrives.
Reading the full transcript before writing a word. Write notes as you go, page by page.
Summarizing from memory. Memory drifts, so check each entry against its page and line.
Letting exhibits slip. Log each exhibit mention on the same row as the testimony that cites it.
Passing the whole job to one reviewer. Split reading from checking so the second person can start sooner.

blocks.text: A simple template avoids most of these problems. Use columns for Page, Line, Topic, Testimony, Exhibit and Follow-up. Save it once in Word or Pages. Reuse it for every deposition, so the format never needs rebuilding.
What AI summary tools can and cannot promise

Several deposition products run as web services. Check each vendor's site for Mac support, pricing and data terms before you trial one. A long feature list does not prove the tool handles your transcript format.

AI can speed up a first draft. It cannot tell you what a witness meant. Accuracy is the risk that matters most. In a 2024 study, leading legal research tools hallucinated between 17 and 33% of the time. That study tested research tools, not deposition summarizers, so the rate for summary tools is unknown.
The ABA's 2024 survey points the same way. Of the attorneys surveyed, 75% named accuracy as their top AI concern. Plan for checking time. A fast draft that needs a full re-read saves very little.
Protect client data before you paste a transcript

A transcript is client data. Your firm or employer sets the rules on which tools may see it. Follow those rules before you paste, upload or dictate case facts into any app. No article can make that decision for you.

Data privacy is a common worry too. In the ABA survey, 47% named data privacy or security as an AI concern. Ask IT whether a tool is approved. Ask whether it stores audio, text or screenshots. Read the vendor's policy, not the homepage.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are Lazur's stated terms, and they do not replace your firm's rules.
Where Lazur fits in a deposition summary

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time.

That covers three jobs in a summary. It explains a Word or Pages screen when you forget where a setting lives. It drafts a template or a follow-up note and types it at your cursor. It answers questions about what is on screen. See the [Word page](/apps/word) for the details.

Lazur works from the screen you have open when you ask. It does not read a 200-page file in one pass. Treat any summary it gives you as a draft, and check it against the transcript before you rely on it.
Dictate your notes while you read

Reading and typing at once slows most people down. Dictate instead. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Say the page, the line and the note, in that order. Dictation is unlimited on both Lazur plans.

Pages has its own dictation. Go to Edit > Start Dictation, speak, and click Done below the microphone to finish. Apple's guide describes live dictation into a document. It does not say Pages transcribes an audio file, so do not count on that.

Voice Memos can transcribe recorded speech on a Mac where transcription is available. Apple notes that it is not available in all countries or regions. Use it for your own voice notes. Check the recording rules for depositions and client calls before you record anything.
Edge cases that add days

items: Speakers who talk over each other. Mark those lines and check the audio before you cite them.
Errata sheets. A correction can change an answer. Log it on the same row as the original line.
Exhibits referenced but missing from the file. Log them as missing, so no one assumes they are attached.
Multi-day depositions. Keep one template across all days, and label each day's pages clearly.
Objections with instructions not to answer. Note who objected, what was said, and whether the witness answered.

blocks.text: Check the summary before it leaves your desk

Spot-check, do not skim. Pick a handful of entries at random and open the transcript to each page and line. If one cite is wrong, check the rest of that section. Wrong names, dates and exhibit numbers do the most damage.
Use the Find bar. In Word or Pages, press ⌘F, type a name, and step through each mention. This takes minutes. It catches the errors a quick read misses.
What the research says about time savings

Research on AI and lawyers is early. A randomized trial of law students found productivity gains of 50 to 130% in five of six legal tasks. The abstract gives no sample size. It does not show how much time a deposition summary would save. Read the study as a sign that tools can help, not as proof for your desk.
Begin with the template and the page count. Once you have a real reading speed, the math tells you how far ahead to start.

faq.question: How long does it take to summarize a 3-hour deposition?
faq.answer: Vendor estimates put a paralegal summary at 8 to 12 hours for a 3-hour deposition. We found no independent study that measures this. Use the figure to plan, then time your own first deposition to build a baseline.

faq.question: How many pages can a paralegal summarize per hour?
faq.answer: One paralegal blog cites 20 to 25 pages an hour as an industry average, without naming a source. Your speed depends on the transcript, your template and how many exhibits come up. Time one section to measure your own pace.

faq.question: How much does a deposition summary cost?
faq.answer: Paralegal Bootcamp estimates $800 to $2,200 for a 200-page transcript at $100 to $220 an hour. Check your firm's billing rates before you quote a client a figure, since your rates may differ.

faq.question: Can AI summarize a deposition on a Mac?
faq.answer: Several deposition products run as web services. Check each vendor's site for Mac support and data terms. Lazur works from the screen you have open when you ask, so it reads one page at a time, not a whole file.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste a transcript into an AI app?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules on client data first. Your firm decides which tools may see case files. Read the vendor's policy on storage and training before you upload anything, and ask IT if you are unsure.

faq.question: Does Lazur summarize whole transcripts?
faq.answer: No, Lazur is not a deposition tool. It answers about what is on screen when you hold ⌥ ⌘, explains menus, dictates notes and drafts text. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Does Pages transcribe an audio file?
faq.answer: Apple's Pages guide describes live dictation into a document. It does not say Pages transcribes audio files. For recorded speech, Voice Memos can transcribe on a Mac where transcription is available.

faq.question: What does Lazur cost, and is it on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. There is a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card, starting when you first open the app. Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 150 AI actions.

costs.title: Paralegal hours
costs.text: A paralegal summary of a 3-hour deposition takes 8 to 12 hours, according to the MedicalAI.law blog. The same post puts a 200-page transcript at more than 8 hours. These are vendor estimates without cited sources.

costs.title: Dollars per transcript
costs.text: Paralegal Bootcamp estimates $800 to $2,200 for a 200-page transcript at $100 to $220 an hour. Its reading speed of 20 to 25 pages an hour is labeled an industry average, with no source named.

costs.title: Attorney review time
costs.text: MedicalAI.law puts lead counsel review at 15 to 25 hours and associate review at 10 to 20 hours. Its plaintiff-side paralegal rate is $75 to $100 an hour, and associate rates are $250 to $400 an hour. Those are one blog's numbers, not a survey.

costs.title: Calendar delay
costs.text: The same MedicalAI.law post puts standard transcript turnaround at 7 to 14 business days. That delay happens before anyone summarizes, so the clock starts earlier than the work does.

costs.title: Errors that cost a second pass
costs.text: A wrong page cite or a missed correction forces a second read. No independent study we found measures how often this happens in deposition summaries, so plan for some rework.

causes.title: A transcript is read in one line
causes.text: A transcript runs top to bottom, and each answer depends on the question before it. Splitting one witness's testimony across three readers loses that context. So the work tends to stay with one person, and that person sets the pace.

causes.title: A summary needs cites, not just a read
causes.text: A useful summary includes page and line cites, exhibit references and notes on objections. Each cite is a second check. Reading turns into reading plus indexing, which takes more time than a plain read.

causes.title: Every team has its own format
causes.text: Each attorney has a preferred layout. Without a shared template, the paralegal builds the format from scratch. Then the reviewer asks for a change, and the draft gets rebuilt.

causes.title: The transcript arrives late
causes.text: A reporter has to certify and deliver the transcript before anyone can summarize it. The MedicalAI.law example gives 7 to 14 business days for standard turnaround. You cannot start earlier than the file exists.

causes.title: Review loops add days
causes.text: A summary often passes through an associate, then a partner. Each reviewer checks the cites again. Busy reviewers take days, and each loop restarts the clock on the draft.

causes.title: Accuracy checks take time
causes.text: Accuracy is the top AI worry for attorneys, at 75% in the ABA's 2024 survey. Teams that use AI for drafts must check every cite. That checking adds review time, even when the draft arrives fast.

fixes.title: Build one template before the transcript arrives
fixes.text: Create a summary template in Word or Pages with columns for Page, Line, Topic, Testimony, Exhibit and Follow-up. Save it once. Reuse it for every deposition, so readers never rebuild the format.

fixes.title: Summarize as you read
fixes.text: Write one row per topic change, not one per page. Keep the page and line on every row. Notes written during the read take less time than a summary rebuilt afterward.

fixes.title: Split reading from checking
fixes.text: Let one person read and draft, and let a second person spot-check the cites. Two short passes fit into busy days better than one long pass with a review at the end.

fixes.title: Log exhibits and objections before you read
fixes.text: Before reading, list every exhibit the parties mark. As you read, tick off each mention. Missing exhibits show up on the list, not in the final draft, and objections get a row of their own.

fixes.title: Protect the reading time on your calendar
fixes.text: Block a session for each stretch of the transcript. Put the transcript's due date in Apple Reminders. Protected blocks finish faster than work squeezed around other tasks.

fixes.title: Verify names and dates with the Find bar
fixes.text: In Word or Pages, press ⌘F to search each name, date and exhibit number. Step through every mention. This catches typos and missed mentions in minutes.

fixes.title: Ask the reporter about turnaround when you book
fixes.text: Ask what turnaround and delivery options the reporter offers, and what they cost. Confirm those details before you set a summary date, because they decide your start day.

fixes.title: Dictate notes instead of typing them
fixes.text: Hold fn and say the page, the line and the note. Dictation keeps your eyes on the transcript. Check names and punctuation after you speak, before the note goes into the summary.

fixes.title: Check every AI line against the transcript
fixes.text: If you use an AI tool, assume a line may be wrong until you find its cite. The 17 to 33% range from the research study is the reason. Open the page, read the line, then keep or fix the entry.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Log the transcript and open the template
plan.text: When the transcript is due, write the due date in Reminders. Open your Word or Pages template and check the columns. List the exhibits the parties marked, if the list is ready.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Read and dictate in blocks
plan.text: Read one section at a time. Dictate each topic with its page and line. Stop at a natural break, so the next block is easy to pick up when you return.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Finish the read and track objections
plan.text: Finish the transcript and log every objection on its own row. Mark speakers who talk over each other, and flag those lines for an audio check.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Draft the summary
plan.text: Turn your notes into a summary grouped by topic. Keep page and line cites in every row. Use Find (⌘F) to confirm names, dates and exhibit numbers.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Spot-check against the transcript
plan.text: Open the transcript to a random set of entries and confirm each cite. If one fails, re-check the whole section before you go further.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Review and send through firm channels
plan.text: Send the draft to your reviewer through the firm's approved system. Log the delivery date. Confirm the data rules before you share anything outside the team.
